what_its_for: Sucralfate is used to treat and prevent ulcers in your stomach and the upper part of your small intestine (duodenal ulcers). It works by forming a protective coating over the ulcer, like a bandage, to help it heal and protect it from stomach acid.
how_to_take: Take sucralfate on an EMPTY STOMACH, at least 1 hour BEFORE meals and at bedtime. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water (8 ounces). If you are using the liquid form, shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring device provided. Do NOT crush or chew the tablets.
dosing: The usual adult dose for an active ulcer is 1 gram (one tablet or 10 mL of liquid) taken 4 times a day — once before each meal and once at bedtime. For preventing an ulcer from coming back, the usual dose is 1 gram twice a day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose may be different.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still at least 1 hour before your next meal. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store sucralfate tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do NOT freeze the liquid form. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids within 30 minutes BEFORE or AFTER taking sucralfate, as they can reduce how well it works. Sucralfate can also interfere with the absorption of many other medications including certain antibiotics (like ciprofloxacin), thyroid medications (like levothyroxine), digoxin, phenytoin, and warfarin. Take those other medications at least 2 hours BEFORE taking sucralfate. Ask your pharmacist if you are unsure about your other medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe constipation or stomach pain that does not go away, signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of your face or throat, or difficulty breathing, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, or if your ulcer symptoms do not improve or get worse after a few weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel some relief from pain and discomfort within a few days of starting sucralfate. However, it is very important to keep taking it for the full length of time prescribed by your doctor (usually 4 to 8 weeks), even if you feel better. Stopping too early may allow the ulcer to come back.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Use sucralfate with caution if you have kidney disease, because it contains aluminum which can build up in the body. Talk to your doctor before using it. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to constipation caused by this medication. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Sucralfate is generally considered low risk in pregnancy, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before taking this medication. Children: Safety and dosing in children should be determined by a doctor.
